items.description: Sec. 4.1.1 says 'the left boundary is clamped' but gives Γ_D = {0}×(−0.5,0.5). In Ω = (−1,1)×(−0.5,0.5) the left edge is x = −1; x = 0 is the vertical mid-span line. Pointing to x = −1: the 3D counterpart (Γ_D = {−1}×…), the offset case ('keeping the left boundary clamped') and the truss-like cantilever layouts reported. Taken literally, x = 0 leaves the left half unsupported, and since β|Ω| = 1 equals the area of the right half, the problem becomes almost degenerate. Fig. 4 might settle it but is not available.
readings: Clamp u_x = u_y = 0 on the whole left edge x = −1, y ∈ [−0.5, 0.5] (0 × length from the left end)
Clamp along the internal vertical line x = 0, y ∈ [−0.5, 0.5] (0.5 × length, mid-span), as literally written

items.entity: Downward load on the right edge (Γ_N)
items.description: Sec. 4.1.1 calls it a 'downward point load' yet puts it on the segment Γ_N = {1}×(−0.05,0.05), which is 10% of the edge height. Eqs. (3.16)–(3.17) integrate t over Γ_N as a traction, and Sec. 4.1.4 samples n_Γ = 500 points on this 'non-homogeneous Neumann boundary'. The 3D analogue, however, is applied 'on the point (1,0,0)'. A grid solver must choose between a nodal force and a patch traction.
readings: Uniform traction on x = 1 over y ∈ [−0.05, 0.05], i.e. 0.45–0.55 of the height (10% patch), lumped consistently to the patch nodes
Single concentrated nodal force at (1, 0), i.e. at 0.5 of the height on the right edge

items.description: t = (0,−1)ᵀ is written as a traction density; over the 0.1-long Γ_N that gives a resultant of 0.1, while 'point load' suggests a unit force. Sec. 4 doesn't say whether the equal-weight Monte Carlo boundary sum carries |Γ_N|. The resultant is never stated. Beam theory gives a solid 2×1 cantilever with E = 1 a compliance of ≈35–40 per unit load², so Table 3's J ≈ 0.60 (APF-FNN) and 0.69 (FEM-PF) suggest a resultant of about 0.1. In a volume-constrained solver this only scales compliance (∝F²). In the paper's unnormalised loss (3.17), though, it also changes the weight of the GL and penalty terms relative to compliance.
readings: Traction 1 per unit length over the 0.1-long patch → resultant 0.1 downward
Resultant 1 downward (unit point load, or traction 10 per unit length over the patch)

items.entity: 2D stress state (plane strain vs plane stress)
items.description: Sec. 3.2.1 builds C0 from the 3D Lamé constant λ = Eν/((1+ν)(1−2ν)) acting on the 2D strain, which is plane strain. Neither Sec. 3.2.1 nor Sec. 4.1.1 names the 2D assumption, and structured-grid compliance codes usually default to plane stress. With ν = 0.3, plane strain equals plane stress with E′ ≈ 1.10 and ν′ ≈ 0.43, so both the stiffness scale and the effective Poisson ratio change.
readings: Plane strain with the given formulas: λ ≈ 0.577, μ ≈ 0.385
Plane stress: λ* = Eν/(1−ν²) ≈ 0.330, μ ≈ 0.385

items.description: No out-of-plane thickness is given for the 2D cases (Secs. 3.2.1, 4.1.1). A plane-stress element stiffness needs one; it multiplies the stiffness and so only scales compliance (∝1/t).
readings: t = 1 (unit thickness / per unit depth)
Other user-chosen thickness t (compliance ∝ 1/t)

items.entity: Analysis/design grid resolution and element type
items.description: APF-FNN is mesh-free. Case (a) uses |X| = 2×10^4 tensor-grid collocation points (Sec. 4.1.2), which Sec. 4.1.4 gives as (n_x, n_y) = (200, 100); nodes vs cell centres is not said. The only FE mesh in the paper is the FEM-PF baseline's 120×60 (Sec. 4.1.3), with no element type, even though the setups are called 'identical'. The ε = 0.01 interface is about one element wide on either grid, while Sec. 1 says it must be resolved by several elements.
readings: 200 × 100 square Q4 elements (h = 0.01), matching the collocation grid behind the reported result
120 × 60 elements (h ≈ 0.0167), as in the FEM-PF baseline
Finer grid, e.g. 400 × 200 (h = 0.005), to resolve the ε = 0.01 interface over several elements (Sec. 4.1.4 also tested 400 × 200 points)

items.entity: Length-scale control: Ginzburg–Landau term vs density/sensitivity filter
items.description: There is no density or sensitivity filter. Length-scale control comes from the Ginzburg–Landau term (Eq. 2.2, W = φ²(1−φ)²/4, ε = γ = 0.01), added unnormalised to the compliance in Eq. (3.17), plus the implicit smoothing of the band-limited Fourier phase field. No filter type or radius is given for a SIMP-type grid solver, and Sec. 4.1.4/Fig. 9 shows the layout changes strongly with (ε, γ). Because the GL weight is absolute, its effect also depends on the compliance scale and on how the Monte Carlo integrals are normalised.
readings: No filter: add γ∫(ε/2·|∇φ|² + φ²(1−φ)²/(4ε))dx with ε = γ = 0.01 directly to the compliance
Density filter with r_min ≈ 1.5 element widths (≈0.015 on 200×100, ≈0.025 on 120×60)
Density/Helmholtz filter with physical radius tied to the interface width, r_min ≈ 2–4ε = 0.02–0.04
Sensitivity filter with r_min ≈ 1.5 element widths

items.entity: Fourier bandwidths ω_max^φ (topology) and ω_max^u (state) for case (a)
items.description: Table 2 and Sec. 4.1.2: ω_max^u = 35, ω_max^φ = 30. Sec. 4.1.4 calls the 'reference setting of case (a)' ω_max^φ = 35, ω_max^u = 30, and the Fig. 13 caption mislabels the pair. Sec. 4.1.4 shows ω_max^φ sets how much fine detail the design has, i.e. an implicit length scale a grid re-run would have to mimic. Units are also inconsistent: Eq. (3.1) uses 2πBx, Eq. (3.4) uses xᵀK with no 2π. The shortest phase-field wavelength is therefore either ≈2π/30 ≈ 0.21 or ≈1/30 ≈ 0.033.
readings: ω_max^φ = 30, ω_max^u = 35 rad per unit length (Table 2, Sec. 4.1.2, Eq. 3.4)
ω_max^φ = 35, ω_max^u = 30 rad per unit length (Sec. 4.1.4)
Either pair read as cycles per unit length, i.e. with the 2π factor of Eq. (3.1)

items.description: β = 0.5 is imposed only softly, through λ_penal(∫φ − β|Ω|)² (Eq. 3.18). For case (a), the initial λ_penal is given only as 'O(1)': Table 2 omits it, while Table 5 gives (1, 0.98) for the eigenvalue cases. ζ = 0.98 is called a 'multiplicative factor' though Algorithm 1 divides by ζ, and only dividing reaches the stated O(10^3–10^4). The final volume can therefore deviate slightly from 0.5. The FEM-PF penalty update is not given.
readings: Hard constraint Σρ_e v_e = 0.5|Ω| (OC/MMA), the natural choice for a volume-constrained solver
Quadratic penalty with λ0 = 1, λ ← λ/0.98 every outer iteration (≈2.4×10^4 after 500)
Quadratic penalty with λ0 = 0.1, λ ← λ/0.98 (≈2.4×10^3 after 500)

items.entity: Design-update scheme and iteration budget for a grid-based re-run
items.description: The reported design comes from Adam updates of a neural phase field (LR 1e-3, N = 500, K = 20, M = 1→10 after n > 200), which has no direct OC/MMA equivalent. The grid baseline (Sec. 4.1.3, FEM-PF: semi-implicit L² Allen–Cahn flow after [21], 100 outer × 20 inner steps) omits the pseudo-time step, element type and penalty update, and it cites a non-existent 'Section 2.3'. Table 3 and Fig. 8 show the two schemes reach different designs (J = 0.5953 vs 0.6930) on 'identical' setups, so the update scheme matters.
readings: Standard OC or MMA, hard volume constraint, run to convergence (e.g. max density change < 0.01)
FEM-PF-style L² Allen–Cahn gradient flow: 100 outer × 20 inner semi-implicit steps with a user-chosen time step
Fixed 500 design iterations to mirror the APF-FNN outer-loop budget
